title: How Humans and Machines Shape Decisions
subject: AI-Literacy
chapter: 13. How Humans and Machines Shape Decisions
description: Practice on how humans keep control and responsibility when using smart devices and AI — from everyday scenarios like smart fridges and doorbells, to deciding which tasks humans vs. machines should lead, using AI for creative writing and health tracking, AI helping (not replacing) teachers, and how programmers stay in control while using GitHub Copilot.

questions.question: What does the worksheet's question 'Is there human agency in the digital world?' ask us to think about?
options: Whether humans still make important decisions and choices even when they use digital tools and AI
Whether computers can grow like plants
Whether humans should stop using any technology
Whether AI is the same thing as a robot toy
questions.explanation: 'Human agency' means a person's own ability to make choices and decisions. This worksheet explores whether people still hold that power even when smart devices and AI are helping with a task.

questions.question: When coding a school quiz app, who actually sets the topics and questions?
options: You input topics & answers
The app guesses topics on its own
The quiz app creates them without any help
No one — the questions appear randomly
questions.explanation: Even a smart quiz app needs a human to decide what topics and questions to include. The app can display or organize a quiz, but a person supplies the actual content.

questions.question: A school quiz app can invent its own topics and questions completely on its own, with no human input at all.
questions.explanation: The 'smartest answer' in the worksheet is that YOU (a human) input the topics and answers — the app does not create meaningful questions entirely by itself.

questions.question: A smart fridge sends a message saying 'Buy milk, it's over.' Who is really responsible for there being milk in the fridge in the first place?
options: The family, because they buy and place items in the fridge
The fridge, because it places orders on its own
The milkman, because he delivers milk every day without anyone asking
No one — milk appears in fridges automatically
questions.explanation: The fridge can only notice milk is missing because a human family first bought and stocked it. The 'smart' feature just detects a pattern; a human caused the milk to be there to begin with.

questions.question: A smart fridge can only suggest buying milk because a human already placed milk in it before.
questions.explanation: The fridge's suggestion is based on tracking what was already stocked by the family — it depends on earlier human action, not independent decision-making.

questions.question: A smart doorbell records visitors and sends alerts about 'suspicious activity.' Who has the real responsibility to decide what counts as suspicious for their own home?
options: The homeowner, who sets and can adjust what counts as suspicious
The device's AI alone, with no human input
The company that made the doorbell decides everything permanently
Whoever walks past the door decides for themselves
questions.explanation: Even though the AI detects motion and matches patterns, the homeowner ultimately decides and can adjust what should be treated as suspicious for their own house. The company may provide default settings, but final control belongs to the human user.

questions.question: A doorbell company may set some default 'suspicious activity' patterns, but the homeowner should still be the one with final control.
questions.explanation: Companies often provide starting settings, but the worksheet's theme is that humans (the homeowner) should retain the final say over how such AI features are configured for their own home.

questions.question: Select ALL of these examples where a smart device's helpful message depends on earlier human action or input.
options: A smart fridge suggesting milk because a family stocked it earlier
A quiz app showing questions a person typed in
A doorbell flagging activity based on settings a homeowner chose
A rock rolling down a hill due to gravity, with no device involved
questions.explanation: The fridge, quiz app, and doorbell each depend on something a human did first — stocking items, entering questions, or choosing settings. A rock rolling down a hill involves no device or human input at all.

questions.question: A GPS app suggests the fastest route to school. Who decided the final destination was 'school'?
options: The person, because they entered or chose the destination
The GPS app, because it decides where you need to go
The app knows your schedule without being told
The satellite chooses your destination
questions.explanation: A GPS app can only calculate a route to a destination once a person tells it where they want to go. It assists with the route, but the human still decides the goal.

questions.question: A GPS app can choose your destination for you without you telling it where you want to go.
questions.explanation: A GPS app calculates routes to a destination a person has entered or chosen — it does not decide where you must go.

questions.question: A smart speaker adds 'eggs' to a shopping list when you ask it to. Who is really in control of what gets added?
options: The person, because they spoke the request
The speaker, because it decides what the family needs
No one, since the list fills itself automatically
The store, because it manages every shopping list
questions.explanation: The smart speaker only adds items a person actually asks for — it is a helpful tool that responds to human requests, not one that decides on its own.

questions.question: An autocorrect tool suggests fixing 'recieve' to 'receive.' Who decides whether to accept the suggestion?
options: The person typing, who can accept or reject it
The autocorrect tool alone, with no choice for the person
The phone's manufacturer, from far away
No one — the correction is permanent and cannot be undone
questions.explanation: Autocorrect suggests a change, but the person typing still chooses whether to keep or reject that suggestion.

questions.question: Even when autocorrect suggests a change, a person can still choose to keep their original spelling.
questions.explanation: Autocorrect makes a suggestion, but the person typing retains the final choice over what stays in their text.

questions.question: A translation app translates a sentence for a school project. Who decides if and how it is used in the project?
options: The student, who decides whether and how to use it
The translation app, which controls the whole project
The app's company, from a different country
No one — the project writes itself
questions.explanation: A translation app can help translate text, but a student still decides whether the translation fits the project and how to use it responsibly.

questions.question: A video app recommends what to watch next. Who ultimately decides whether to watch it?
options: The viewer, who can choose to watch or skip it
The app, which forces every recommended video to play
The video's creator, who decides for the viewer
The internet provider, from far away
questions.explanation: A recommendation is just a suggestion — the viewer still has to choose to click play or skip it, keeping their own agency over what they watch.

questions.question: Video and shopping apps can suggest things, but a person still makes the final choice to click or buy.
questions.explanation: Recommendations from apps are suggestions, not final decisions — a person still chooses whether to act on them.

questions.question: A ride-hailing app automatically picks a driver and route. Does this mean the passenger has no say at all?
options: No — the passenger chose to request the ride, picked the destination, and can still cancel or change plans
Yes, the app has full control with no human choice involved
Yes, because computers always make better choices than people
No — but only because passengers are never allowed to cancel
questions.explanation: Even though the app automatically matches a driver and calculates a route, the passenger still made the key choices: requesting the ride, setting the destination, and being able to cancel or change plans.

questions.question: Which of these best defines 'human agency'?
options: A person's ability to make their own choices and take action, even when using digital tools
A robot's ability to think exactly like a human
A rule that says AI must always be used instead of humans
A type of computer chip used inside smart devices
questions.explanation: Human agency is about people's own power to choose and act — this worksheet shows that this power can remain even when AI or smart devices are involved.

questions.question: Select ALL of these that are examples of a smart device ASSISTING a human, rather than fully replacing the human's decision.
options: A fridge suggesting milk based on what was stocked
A GPS app calculating a route to a destination a person chose
Autocorrect suggesting a spelling fix a person can accept or reject
A vending machine deciding your favourite snack for you without asking
questions.explanation: The fridge, GPS, and autocorrect examples all help a person while leaving the final decision with them. A vending machine that decided your favourite snack without asking would be removing your choice entirely, unlike the worksheet's examples.

questions.question: In a photo-editing app, who decides which filter to apply to a photo?
options: The person using the app, who selects the filter they like
The app, which forces one filter on every photo
The camera itself, without any settings
The photo, because it chooses its own style
questions.explanation: A photo app may offer several filters, but the person using it still chooses which one (if any) to apply.

questions.question: Choosing to use an AI tool for a task means you automatically give up all control over the outcome.
questions.explanation: Using an AI tool does not remove a person's control — as the worksheet's examples show, people can still review, choose, and decide how to use what the AI suggests.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the lesson from the quiz-app, fridge, and doorbell examples together?
options: In each case, an earlier human choice or setting shapes what the 'smart' feature does
In each case, the device makes every decision with no human involved at all
In each case, the device is completely useless without a person present at all times
In each case, only the company that built the device has any control
questions.explanation: Across all three examples, the device's helpful behaviour is only possible because a human earlier supplied questions, stocked items, or chose settings — the human's role shapes what the device can do.

questions.question: A student says, 'AI apps always know exactly what I want without me telling them anything.' Is this true, based on the worksheet's examples?
options: No — apps like the quiz app, fridge, and doorbell all depend on information or settings a human provided
Yes, AI apps can read minds directly
Yes, because AI never needs any information from people
No — but only because apps are always broken
questions.explanation: The worksheet's three examples all show that a smart app or device needs some human-provided information or setting first — it cannot simply know what a person wants with no input at all.

questions.question: Select ALL of these that a human must still do, even when using a smart app from the worksheet's examples.
options: Type in the quiz questions and answers
Buy and stock items in the fridge
Choose the doorbell's suspicious-activity settings
Nothing — the app manages everything by itself
questions.explanation: In every example from the worksheet, a human still had to supply questions, stock items, or choose settings — the apps did not manage everything by themselves.

questions.question: A smart speaker sets an alarm when a person asks for it. Who decided the wake-up time?
options: The person who asked for the alarm
The smart speaker, on its own
The electricity company
No one — alarms set themselves randomly
questions.explanation: A smart speaker only sets the alarm a person requests — the wake-up time is the person's own choice, and the speaker just carries it out.

questions.question: As apps become smarter, humans automatically have less and less agency in every situation, with no exceptions.
questions.explanation: The worksheet's examples show that people can keep meaningful agency (choosing, reviewing, deciding) even while using smart apps — agency does not automatically disappear just because a tool is 'smart.'

questions.question: An online shopping app suggests products based on past purchases. Who makes the final decision to buy?
options: The shopper, who reviews the suggestion and decides
The app, which purchases items automatically with no approval
The delivery driver
The product itself
questions.explanation: A shopping app can suggest products, but the shopper still reviews the suggestion and makes the final decision to buy or not.

questions.question: Why is it useful to ask 'who really decides?' whenever we use a smart app or device?
options: It helps us notice that humans usually still make the important decisions, even when a device seems to act on its own
It proves that AI should never be used for anything
It shows that devices always make better choices than humans
It has no real purpose in everyday life
questions.explanation: Asking 'who really decides' helps students notice the hidden human input and control behind seemingly automatic 'smart' behaviour, which is the central lesson of this worksheet.

questions.question: Select ALL statements that are TRUE about human agency, based on the worksheet's examples.
options: Agency means people keep making meaningful choices, even while using AI tools
The fridge, doorbell, and quiz-app examples show hidden human input behind 'smart' behaviour
Human agency completely disappears the moment a person uses any app
Thinking about 'who really decides' helps people notice their own role in a decision
questions.explanation: The worksheet shows agency persisting through human input and choice, not disappearing. 'Agency vanishes with any app use' is false — the fridge, doorbell, and quiz-app examples prove the opposite.

questions.question: What is the opposite idea to 'human agency' in these worksheet examples?
options: Believing a device or AI makes all the important decisions completely by itself
Believing that people should type their own quiz questions
Believing that families stock their own fridges
Believing that homeowners can adjust doorbell settings
questions.explanation: The opposite of human agency would be assuming a device or AI is fully in charge with no human input — which the worksheet's examples show is not actually the case.

questions.question: Which type of task are machines/AI typically best at leading?
options: Repetitive, pattern-based tasks like sorting or recognizing patterns
Understanding someone's feelings
Deciding what is fair between two friends
Comforting a sad friend
questions.explanation: Machines excel at fast, repetitive, pattern-based work like sorting data or recognizing shapes, but they cannot truly understand feelings, fairness, or offer comfort the way a human can.

questions.question: Which type of task should a human typically lead, even if AI can help with parts of it?
options: Understanding an emotional problem between friends
Sorting a long list of names alphabetically
Recognizing repeated shapes in many photos
Predicting a repeating pattern in numbers
questions.explanation: Understanding an emotional problem needs empathy, context, and judgement about people's feelings — something a human is far better suited to lead than a machine.

questions.question: Understanding a problem between two friends is best led by a human, not a machine.
questions.explanation: This kind of task needs empathy and understanding of feelings, which machines do not truly have, so a human should lead it.

questions.question: 'Organizing digital files' is best suited to which kind of leader, and why?
options: A machine, because it is a repetitive, pattern-based task like sorting by name or date
A human, because it requires deep emotional understanding
Neither, because files organize themselves
A human, because computers cannot recognize file names
questions.explanation: Sorting and organizing files by name, type, or date is a repetitive, rule-based task that computers can do quickly and consistently, making it well suited to machine assistance.

questions.question: Recognizing shapes in photos is a task that machines (AI/image recognition) are typically very good at.
questions.explanation: Machines are strong at recognizing visual patterns, such as shapes in photos, because it involves comparing pixel patterns quickly and consistently.

questions.question: 'Ranking tasks by importance' (like a to-do list) is best led by whom, and why?
options: A human, because it depends on personal values and priorities
A machine, because importance is always the same for everyone
Neither, because tasks rank themselves
A machine, because humans cannot judge importance
questions.explanation: What counts as 'important' depends on a person's own goals, values, and situation — something only a human can judge well for themselves.

questions.question: A lunch-ordering app 'suggests' items based on past orders. Who still leads the final decision?
options: The person ordering
The app, which places the order without asking
The restaurant, without any customer input
The delivery driver
questions.explanation: The app can suggest items based on patterns in past orders, but the person ordering still chooses what to actually order.

questions.question: Select ALL tasks from this list that are typically better LED by a machine (because they are pattern-based).
options: Predicting a class schedule change (using data/patterns)
Organizing digital files
Recognizing shapes in photos
Understanding problems between friends
questions.explanation: Predicting patterns, organizing files, and recognizing shapes are all pattern-based tasks machines handle well. Understanding problems between friends needs human empathy, not machine pattern-matching.

questions.question: Select ALL tasks from this list that are typically better LED by a human (because they need judgement or empathy).
options: Ranking tasks by importance
Understanding problems between friends
Recognizing shapes in photos
Organizing digital files by date
questions.explanation: Ranking importance and understanding friends' problems both depend on personal values and empathy, which humans lead best. Recognizing shapes and organizing files are pattern-based tasks machines handle well.

questions.question: Why might 'predicting a class schedule change' be something a machine can help with, even though a human makes the final call?
options: It involves analysing patterns and data, but the actual decision to change a schedule is still made by a school authority
Machines always decide school schedules with no human involvement
It has nothing to do with patterns at all
Schedules never actually change, so this task is meaningless
questions.explanation: A machine can spot patterns in timetable data and suggest a likely change, but a human (like a school administrator) still makes and approves the actual decision.

questions.question: A machine can never help with a task that also needs human judgement.
questions.explanation: The fridge and quiz-app examples show machines can assist with tasks (like flagging missing items or displaying questions) while humans still provide the judgement and final decisions.

questions.question: What is a good general rule for deciding whether a human or a machine should lead a task?
options: Machines are best at repetitive, pattern-based work; humans are best at tasks needing feelings, values, and judgement
Machines should always lead every task, no matter what
Humans should always lead every task, no matter what
There is no difference between what humans and machines can lead
questions.explanation: This general rule (from the worksheet's H/M classification activity) helps explain why some tasks suit machines (patterns, speed) and others suit humans (feelings, values, judgement).

questions.question: A lunch app recommends the same sandwich you always order. Does this mean the app decides what you eat?
options: No — the app only recommends based on a pattern; the person still chooses what to actually order
Yes — the app fully controls what you eat from now on
Yes — because patterns always override personal choice
No — because the app never learns any patterns at all
questions.explanation: A recommendation based on past orders is still just a suggestion; the person ordering keeps the power to choose something different.

questions.question: Select ALL TRUE reasons a machine is well-suited to recognizing shapes in photos.
options: It can quickly compare patterns across many images
It never gets tired of repeating the same check
It understands how a person feels about the photo
It can decide if a photo is meaningful to someone
questions.explanation: Machines are fast and tireless at comparing visual patterns. Understanding feelings or personal meaning requires empathy and context that machines do not truly have.

questions.question: Two students disagree about a made-up rule for a game they invented. Should a machine or a human resolve it?
options: A human, since it needs judgement about fairness and feelings
A machine, since rules are always about numbers and patterns
Neither, since disagreements resolve themselves
A machine, since humans cannot judge fairness
questions.explanation: Resolving a disagreement about fairness in a made-up game requires understanding both people's feelings and perspectives, which is a human strength, not a machine one.

questions.question: Ranking tasks by importance often depends on a person's own values and goals, which a machine cannot fully know.
questions.explanation: What is 'important' varies from person to person based on their goals and values — something a machine cannot fully understand or judge on its own.

questions.question: Which of these is LEAST likely to be something AI can do well entirely on its own?
options: Comforting a friend who is upset
Sorting files by date
Recognizing a shape in an image
Predicting a repeating pattern in data
questions.explanation: Comforting someone requires empathy and genuine understanding of feelings, which AI does not truly have, unlike sorting, recognizing patterns, or predicting trends.

questions.question: A school's timetable tool flags a possible scheduling conflict. What should happen next?
options: A human (teacher or administrator) reviews it and decides the final change
The tool automatically changes everyone's schedule with no review
Nothing, since the tool's flag is always correct
Students should each change their own schedule immediately
questions.explanation: A tool can flag a possible pattern or conflict, but a responsible human should review the situation and make the final scheduling decision.

questions.question: Select ALL of these that require human empathy and cannot be fully replaced by a machine.
options: Understanding problems between friends
Comforting someone who feels upset
Deciding what is fair in a disagreement
Predicting a repeating pattern in a class schedule
questions.explanation: Understanding problems, comforting someone, and judging fairness all require empathy — a human strength. Predicting a repeating pattern is instead a task machines handle well.

questions.question: Why can't a machine fully 'understand' a problem between two friends?
options: Because it requires empathy and understanding feelings, which machines do not truly have
Because friends never have real problems
Because machines are too slow to notice problems
Because problems between friends are always about numbers
questions.explanation: Truly understanding a friendship problem requires empathy — genuinely sensing and caring about how someone feels — which is a human quality machines lack.

questions.question: Even for tasks a machine can help with, like organizing files, a human decided the rules for how the files should be organized.
questions.explanation: A machine can sort files quickly, but a human still sets up the folders, categories, or rules that guide how the sorting should happen.

questions.question: What best describes how humans and machines can work together on a task like predicting a class schedule change?
options: The machine analyses patterns and suggests options; the human makes the final decision
The machine decides everything with no human input
The human ignores the machine's suggestions completely
Neither works on this task at all
questions.explanation: This reflects healthy human-machine teamwork: the machine's pattern analysis supports the decision, but the human retains the authority to decide and approve the final change.

questions.question: Select ALL examples of MACHINE-strength tasks from everyday life.
options: Sorting a list of numbers
Recognizing a face in a photo
Organizing files by size
Choosing a fair way to split chores among friends
questions.explanation: Sorting numbers, recognizing faces, and organizing files by size are all pattern-based tasks machines are good at. Choosing a fair way to split chores needs human judgement about fairness.

questions.question: A group of students argue about whose turn it is to lead a group project fairly. Who should decide?
options: The humans involved (perhaps with a teacher's guidance), since it needs judgement about fairness
An app, since fairness can always be calculated by a computer
No one, since the argument will resolve itself
A machine, because humans are always unfair
questions.explanation: Deciding what is fair between people involves judgement, values, and understanding everyone's perspective — a human strength that a machine cannot replace.

questions.question: Machines are naturally better than humans at understanding emotions and feelings.
questions.explanation: Machines are strong at recognizing patterns and repeating data-based tasks, but they do not truly understand emotions and feelings the way humans do.

questions.question: Which best explains why 'a lunch-ordering app suggesting items' is a machine-assisting task rather than a fully human one?
options: It is based on repeating patterns in past orders, though the final choice to order still remains with the human
It requires deep understanding of a person's feelings
It has nothing to do with patterns at all
It fully removes the human's ability to choose what to eat
questions.explanation: The app's suggestion comes from spotting patterns in past orders (a machine strength), but the person ordering still makes the final choice.

questions.question: A task like sorting hundreds of photos by date is best handled quickly by a ________.
options: machine/computer
feeling
friendship
value
questions.explanation: Sorting many photos by date is a repetitive, pattern-based task, which machines/computers can do quickly and accurately.

questions.question: If a machine leads a repetitive task like organizing files, this means humans have no role in it at all.
questions.explanation: Even when a machine leads a repetitive task, a human still set up the folders or rules and can review the results — humans are not entirely removed from the process.

questions.question: How does the worksheet's 'Who leads?' (H/M) activity help us think about AI?
options: It helps us notice which jobs suit computers' strengths (patterns, speed) and which need human strengths (feelings, values, judgement)
It proves that machines should lead every task in life
It proves that humans should never use machines for anything
It shows that patterns and feelings are exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: Classifying tasks as Human-led or Machine-led builds the habit of recognizing which strengths (speed/patterns vs. feelings/judgement) fit which kind of task.

questions.question: Select ALL statements that are TRUE about human and machine strengths.
options: Machines are fast and consistent at repeating pattern-based tasks
Humans understand feelings and personal values well
Machines never make any mistakes
Humans always work faster than machines at every task
questions.explanation: Machines are indeed fast/consistent at patterns, and humans understand feelings/values well. But machines CAN make mistakes, and humans do not always work faster than machines at pattern-based tasks.

questions.question: What is Alex using AI to help him do?
options: Write a story about friendship
Fix his bicycle
Solve a maths problem
Plan a birthday party
questions.explanation: Alex uses AI to help write a story about friendship, and the worksheet explores how he can stay in control of that creative work.

questions.question: What pattern does Alex notice in the AI's story ideas?
options: The AI always shows characters fixing problems using technology instead of talking to each other
The AI always makes characters become best friends instantly
The AI never gives any ideas at all
The AI always writes about animals
questions.explanation: Alex notices the AI keeps suggesting technology-based solutions to problems, rather than characters resolving things by talking to one another.

questions.question: The AI in Alex's story always suggests that characters solve problems by talking to each other.
questions.explanation: The worksheet says the opposite — the AI keeps suggesting characters use technology to fix problems, not conversation.

questions.question: Why might it matter that the AI keeps suggesting 'technology' solutions instead of 'talking' solutions?
options: Because it may not reflect the values Alex wants his story to teach, like communication and friendship
Because technology solutions are always factually wrong
Because it means the AI is broken
Because it has no effect on the story at all
questions.explanation: If Alex accepts every AI idea without thinking, his story might unintentionally teach a message he doesn't intend — this is why noticing the AI's pattern matters.

questions.question: Alex controls the story's core message, even though the AI provides ideas.
questions.explanation: The AI can suggest ideas, but Alex, as the human writer, is the one who decides the story's core message.

questions.question: What should Alex do to keep his story creative and personal?
options: Choose some AI ideas and add his own thoughts
Use all ideas from the AI without changes
Let the AI finish the story alone
Ask the AI to pick which ideas are best
questions.explanation: Blending some AI ideas with his own thinking lets Alex keep the story creative and personal, rather than letting the AI fully take over.

questions.question: Using ALL of the AI's ideas without changing anything would keep Alex's story most creative and personal.
questions.explanation: The worksheet's answer is the opposite: choosing SOME AI ideas and adding his own thoughts keeps the story creative and personal, not accepting everything unchanged.

questions.question: Why is 'letting the AI finish the story alone' NOT a good choice for Alex?
options: Because then the story would reflect the AI's patterns and ideas, not Alex's own creativity and values
Because AI cannot write any words at all
Because it would make the story too short
Because teachers never allow any AI use
questions.explanation: If Alex lets the AI finish the whole story, the final product reflects the AI's patterns rather than Alex's own creative voice and values.

questions.question: How can Alex use AI in a good way while keeping human values in his story?
options: Use AI only for ideas and write the story himself
Let AI decide how every character behaves
Copy the story exactly as the AI writes it
Have the AI write the whole story and just put his name on it
questions.explanation: Using AI only for ideas — while Alex does the actual writing — keeps the human values and personal voice in the story.

questions.question: Why is 'having the AI write the whole story and just putting his name on it' not honest or a good use of AI?
options: Because it would mean claiming credit for the AI's work, not Alex's own thinking or writing
Because AI stories are always factually incorrect
Because it takes too much time
Because teachers can always tell which app was used
questions.explanation: Submitting AI-generated work as entirely one's own, without doing the thinking or writing, is dishonest — it doesn't reflect Alex's true effort or creativity.

questions.question: It is dishonest to submit AI-written work as entirely your own without doing your own thinking or writing.
questions.explanation: Claiming full credit for work that was actually created by AI, with no real personal effort, is not honest.

questions.question: Select ALL good ways for Alex to use AI while writing his story.
options: Use it for ideas
Add his own thoughts to some AI ideas
Decide the core message himself
Let the AI decide how every character behaves
questions.explanation: Using AI for ideas, adding his own thoughts, and deciding the message himself all keep Alex in control. Letting AI decide how characters behave would hand over creative control entirely.

questions.question: What is the 'core message' of a story?
options: The main idea, lesson, or value the story is trying to share
The number of pages in the story
The font used to print the story
The title of the story only
questions.explanation: A story's core message is its central idea or lesson — something Alex, not the AI, should decide for his own story.

questions.question: What is a possible downside of always following the same kind of 'technology fixes everything' idea from AI?
options: The story might miss other valuable lessons, like the importance of communication and friendship between people
The story would become factually incorrect
The story would be too short to read
There is no downside at all
questions.explanation: If Alex always follows the AI's repeated pattern, his story about friendship might lose an important lesson about people talking and connecting with each other.

questions.question: AI ideas are always neutral and never repeat the same kind of pattern or suggestion.
questions.explanation: The worksheet shows the opposite — the AI keeps repeating the same kind of pattern (technology fixing problems) in its story suggestions to Alex.

questions.question: Which of these best shows Alex keeping human agency while writing his story?
options: Reviewing the AI's ideas and deciding what to keep, change, or reject
Accepting every AI idea without reading it
Letting the AI publish the story without his review
Ignoring the assignment altogether
questions.explanation: Reviewing and choosing what to keep or change from the AI's ideas is exactly how Alex exercises his own human agency in this creative task.

questions.question: Select ALL of these that are examples of AI helping with a creative task, not fully replacing the human creator.
options: Alex uses AI for story ideas but writes the story himself
A programmer uses Copilot for code suggestions but checks them
An AI publishes a whole book with no human author involved
A student edits some AI-suggested ideas before using them
questions.explanation: Alex, the programmer, and the student all stay involved and in control while AI assists. An AI publishing a whole book with no human author would mean full replacement, not assistance.

questions.question: Why should a writer stay involved even when AI can generate lots of ideas quickly?
options: Because the writer's own values, judgement, and creativity are needed to shape a meaningful, personal story
Because AI cannot generate any ideas at all
Because writing takes no time either way
Because AI ideas are always wrong
questions.explanation: Speed of idea generation doesn't replace the human judgement and personal creativity needed to shape a story that truly reflects the writer's own values.

questions.question: Getting ideas from AI means Alex should stop thinking for himself.
questions.explanation: The worksheet teaches the opposite — Alex should use AI ideas as a starting point while still doing his own thinking, choosing, and writing.

questions.question: Which best matches 'using AI in a good way' as taught in this worksheet?
options: Using AI as a helper for ideas while the human keeps control of the final work
Using AI to replace all human effort completely
Never using AI for any part of a task
Letting AI decide the final grade for the work
questions.explanation: The worksheet consistently teaches that AI is best used as a helper, with the human keeping control of decisions and the final product.

questions.question: Alex could ask the AI to write the entire story exactly as it suggests. What would this risk losing?
options: Alex's own creativity, personal voice, and the human values he wants the story to show
Nothing, since AI stories are always identical to human-written ones
Only the story's length
Only the story's title

questions.explanation: The worksheet lists deciding the program's purpose, checking correctness, and fixing mistakes as the programmer's responsibilities — not handing over the whole project with no oversight.

questions.question: Why is Copilot compared to how a phone predicts words?
options: Because both suggest the 'next' piece (a word or a line of code) based on patterns, but the human decides whether to accept it
Because phones and computers are made of the exact same materials
Because both tools cost the same amount of money
Because phones and Copilot were invented on the same day
questions.explanation: Both word prediction and Copilot's code suggestions work by predicting a likely 'next' piece from patterns, while the human decides whether to accept the suggestion.

questions.question: Which best explains why Copilot helps programmers 'work faster'?
options: It takes care of boring, repeated coding tasks so programmers can focus on more important work
It replaces the need for programmers to write any code at all
It makes computers run at a higher speed
It removes the need for the internet
questions.explanation: By handling repeated, boring parts of coding, Copilot frees up programmers to spend time on more important thinking and decisions.

questions.question: Even though Copilot suggests code, the final responsibility for what the program does rests with the human programmer.
questions.explanation: The worksheet emphasizes that programmers decide what the program should do and are responsible for checking and fixing the code.

questions.question: How is the Copilot example similar to the fridge and doorbell examples earlier in the worksheet?
options: In each case, an AI tool assists with a task, but a human still makes the important decisions and checks the results
In each case, the AI fully replaces the human with no oversight
In each case, no human is involved at any point
In each case, the task is impossible for either a human or a machine
questions.explanation: Across all these examples, AI assists (suggesting code, flagging milk, detecting activity), but a human retains the final decision-making role.

questions.question: Copilot acts like a helpful AI ________ while programmers write code.
options: partner
replacement
teacher
customer
questions.explanation: The worksheet describes Copilot as working 'like a helpful AI partner' during coding, not as a replacement for the programmer.

questions.question: Select ALL of these that describe what a programmer does, even while using Copilot.
options: Decides what the program should do
Checks AI suggestions
Fixes mistakes
Lets the AI publish the final program without any review
questions.explanation: The worksheet describes programmers deciding, checking, and fixing — not publishing AI code without any review.

questions.question: Copilot can completely replace the need for a human programmer to think about the code.
questions.explanation: The worksheet is clear that programmers are always in control, thinking carefully and checking Copilot's suggestions.

questions.question: What does the worksheet suggest happens if a programmer blindly trusts every Copilot suggestion?
options: Mistakes may go unnoticed, since Copilot is not always right
The program will always run perfectly with no issues
Copilot will stop working entirely
The programmer will automatically become an expert
questions.explanation: Blindly trusting suggestions skips the checking step the worksheet emphasizes, risking unnoticed mistakes since Copilot is not always right.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of GitHub Copilot, according to the worksheet?
options: To help programmers write code faster by suggesting lines and handling repeated tasks
To replace the internet entirely
To design video games automatically
To translate languages for websites
questions.explanation: The worksheet's passage describes Copilot's purpose as helping programmers write code faster through suggestions and handling repeated tasks.

questions.question: According to the worksheet, using an AI coding assistant like Copilot means programmers no longer need to understand their own code.
questions.explanation: The worksheet says the opposite — programmers must think carefully, check suggestions, and fix mistakes, which requires understanding their own code.

questions.question: Which best summarizes the overall lesson of the GitHub Copilot passage?
options: AI tools can make repetitive work faster, but humans must still think carefully, check the AI's work, and make the final decisions
AI tools always make fewer mistakes than any human programmer
Programmers no longer need any coding skills once they use AI tools
Copilot works completely independently of any human programmer
questions.explanation: This captures the passage's balanced message: AI speeds up repetitive work, but humans remain responsible for thinking, checking, and deciding.

questions.question: Select ALL of these that are examples of 'boring, repeated tasks' an AI coding assistant might help with.
options: Suggesting common lines of code
Auto-completing familiar coding patterns
Deciding the entire purpose and design of a brand-new app
Filling in code that follows a pattern already used elsewhere
questions.explanation: Suggesting common lines, auto-completing patterns, and filling in repeated code patterns are the kind of repetitive tasks Copilot helps with. Deciding an app's entire purpose and design needs human thinking, not repetitive pattern-matching.

questions.question: Is GitHub Copilot used by only a small number of specialised experts, according to the worksheet?
options: No, it is used by millions of programmers
Yes, only ten people in the world use it
Yes, only students are allowed to use it
No, no one actually uses it
questions.explanation: The worksheet states that millions of computer programmers use GitHub Copilot, not just a small group of experts.

questions.question: How does the GitHub Copilot example connect to the chapter's overall theme of 'human agency'?
options: It shows that even with a helpful AI tool, humans (programmers) remain in control of decisions, correctness, and the final code
It shows that AI tools always remove all human control completely
It shows that coding has nothing to do with human decision-making
It shows that human agency only applies to non-technology examples
questions.explanation: Like the other examples in the worksheet, Copilot shows AI assisting while the human retains control, correctness checks, and the final decision — reinforcing the chapter's human agency theme.

questions.question: Across the quiz app, fridge, doorbell, story-writing, health app, teacher, and Copilot examples, what is the CONSISTENT lesson?
options: Humans should stay involved and make the important decisions, even when AI or smart devices help
Machines should always take over every decision permanently
Humans and machines never interact in real life
AI should be avoided completely in every situation
questions.explanation: Every example in the worksheet — from the fridge to Copilot — repeats the same lesson: AI can help, but humans should keep the important decisions.

questions.question: What is a good habit to build when using any smart app or AI tool, based on this worksheet?
options: Pause and ask 'who is really making the decision here?' and stay involved
Accept every suggestion immediately without thinking
Assume the app always knows better than you
Stop using technology altogether
questions.explanation: This reflective habit — asking who is really deciding — is exactly what each scenario in the worksheet trains students to do.

questions.question: This worksheet's overall message is that AI should always fully replace human decision-making.
questions.explanation: The worksheet's message is the opposite — humans should stay involved and keep control, even while using helpful AI tools.

questions.question: What does it mean for a human to have 'oversight' of an AI tool?
options: To review, guide, and check the AI's work or suggestions, rather than accepting them blindly
To never look at what the AI produces
To let the AI make every decision with no review at all
To avoid using any AI tool ever again
questions.explanation: Oversight means actively reviewing and guiding an AI's suggestions or actions, rather than passively accepting them without question.

questions.question: Select ALL examples from the worksheet where a human's oversight or input was shown to matter.
options: Choosing quiz questions
Stocking the fridge
Setting doorbell preferences
A rock falling due to gravity
questions.explanation: Choosing quiz questions, stocking the fridge, and setting doorbell preferences are all worksheet examples of human input mattering. A rock falling due to gravity involves no human or AI decision at all.

questions.question: Why does the worksheet keep returning to 'who decides' or 'who leads' in each scenario?
options: To help students build the habit of thinking critically about the role of humans versus AI in everyday decisions
Because it is the only question the worksheet can ask
Because it has no connection to AI literacy at all
Because the answer is always the same for every scenario, so it doesn't matter
questions.explanation: Repeating the 'who decides'/'who leads' question across different scenarios builds the habit of critically examining human vs. AI roles in everyday life.

questions.question: In every example in this worksheet, the AI tool works completely alone with no information or setting from a human.
questions.explanation: Every example (fridge, doorbell, quiz app, Copilot, health app) shows the AI depending on some human-provided information or setting.

questions.question: Which best defines the term 'AI' as it is used across these examples?
options: A computer system/program that can perform tasks like suggesting, predicting, or recognizing patterns, often to assist people
A type of physical robot that looks like a human
A brand of smartphone
A subject taught only in university
questions.explanation: Across the worksheet's examples (fridge, doorbell, Copilot, health app), AI refers to software that assists with suggesting, predicting, or recognizing patterns.

questions.question: Why is it important for young learners to understand ideas like 'human agency' and 'oversight' early on?
options: So they can use AI and smart devices thoughtfully and responsibly instead of just trusting them blindly
So they can avoid all technology for the rest of their lives
So they can build robots themselves at a young age
So they never have to think about decisions again
questions.explanation: Understanding these ideas early helps students grow into thoughtful, responsible users of technology who question and check AI rather than blindly trusting it.

questions.question: Select ALL of the following that are examples of AI ASSISTING rather than fully deciding, according to this worksheet.
options: Fridge suggesting milk
Doorbell flagging activity
Copilot suggesting code
An app locking a family out of their own house with no human control at all
questions.explanation: The fridge, doorbell, and Copilot all assist while humans keep control. An app locking a family out with no human control would be an example of AI fully overriding human agency, which is not what the worksheet endorses.

questions.question: In the worksheet's Company A vs. Company B example, which idea reflects 'AI assisting humans' rather than 'AI replacing humans'?
options: Company B's idea
Company A's idea
Both ideas equally
Neither idea involves AI at all
questions.explanation: Company B's idea (AI helping teachers with small jobs) reflects assisting humans, while Company A's idea (AI replacing teachers) reflects full replacement.

questions.question: Copilot, the fridge, the doorbell, and the health app are all examples of AI tools mentioned in this worksheet.
questions.explanation: All four are AI-related examples used across the worksheet's different scenarios.

questions.question: Why does the worksheet use everyday examples like fridges and doorbells instead of only complicated ones?
options: To help students see that questions about human agency and AI apply to ordinary devices they may already use, not just advanced technology
Because complicated examples are too expensive to describe
Because fridges and doorbells are the only devices that use AI
Because everyday examples have nothing to teach about AI
questions.explanation: Using familiar, everyday examples helps students connect the chapter's ideas about human agency to devices they may already encounter in daily life.

questions.question: Why does 'circle the smartest answer' (not just any true answer) matter in the worksheet's first question?
options: Because more than one option might seem partly true, but only one best reflects that humans, not the device, hold the real responsibility
Because there is no correct answer to the question
Because every option given is equally correct
Because the question has nothing to do with responsibility
questions.explanation: The 'smartest answer' phrasing signals that among plausible-sounding options, only one best captures the worksheet's key idea about human responsibility.

questions.question: Select ALL scenarios in the worksheet where a HUMAN needed to give approval, input, or final judgement.
options: Quiz questions
Fridge stocking
Doorbell settings
AI fully replacing every human role with no oversight, as claimed by Company A
questions.explanation: Quiz questions, fridge stocking, and doorbell settings all needed human input or judgement. Company A's idea of AI fully replacing every human role with no oversight was presented as the worse option, not something the worksheet endorses as needing human approval.

questions.question: The worksheet's title question, 'Is there human agency in the digital world?', is answered with a clear 'yes' across its examples.
questions.explanation: Every scenario in the worksheet shows humans retaining meaningful control and decision-making, answering the title question with a clear 'yes.'

questions.question: What should you do if you're not sure whether to trust an AI's suggestion, based on this worksheet's lessons?
options: Think it over, check it against what you know, and ask a trusted human (like a parent, teacher, or doctor) if needed
Always accept it immediately, no matter what
Ignore it completely without even reading it
Ask another AI tool to decide for you
questions.explanation: The worksheet's repeated lesson is to think critically, check suggestions, and involve trusted humans when needed, rather than blindly accepting or ignoring AI.

questions.question: Which best explains the connection between the Copilot example and the Alex story-writing example?
options: Both show a human staying in control and checking the AI's suggestions rather than accepting them without question
Both show AI completely replacing the human with no review
Both have nothing to do with checking suggestions
Both are about health data, not creativity or code
questions.explanation: In both examples, a human (the programmer or Alex) reviews AI suggestions and decides what to keep, change, or reject, keeping control of the final result.

questions.question: Select ALL of these that are examples of 'thinking deeper' activities in the worksheet.
options: The mind map about teachers and AI
Deciding which company's idea is better
Explaining why an idea is better for schools
A multiple choice question with no discussion at all
questions.explanation: The mind map, deciding which idea is better, and explaining why are all part of the worksheet's 'Thinking deeper' section, which invites reasoning and discussion.

questions.question: A student claims, 'Since AI is very smart, humans don't need to check its work anymore.' Based on this worksheet, is this a fair conclusion?
options: No, because the worksheet repeatedly shows that AI can be wrong or incomplete, so human review matters
Yes, since AI is always correct in every situation
Yes, because checking AI's work wastes time
No, but only because AI is never actually smart at all
questions.explanation: The worksheet repeatedly shows AI can be incomplete or wrong (Copilot's mistakes, the AI story's repeated pattern), so human review remains important.

questions.question: According to this worksheet, both machines and humans can play useful roles in making decisions, as long as humans keep the final say on important matters.
questions.explanation: This balanced idea reflects the worksheet's overall message across all its scenarios — machines assist, but humans keep the final, important decisions.

questions.question: What is one way a person can practice good 'human agency' when using any AI app?
options: Reviewing suggestions before accepting them and making the final choice themselves
Accepting every suggestion instantly without thinking
Letting the app make every decision permanently
Deleting the app without ever trying it
questions.explanation: Reviewing and choosing, rather than blindly accepting, is exactly how a person exercises their own human agency with any AI app.

questions.question: Why does this worksheet compare AI's code suggestions to smart phone word predictions?
options: To help students understand a complex AI idea (code suggestions) using something familiar (word prediction) they've likely already seen
Because phones and computers are exactly the same device
Because word prediction and coding have no similarities at all
Because it is required by the app's terms of use
questions.explanation: Comparing an unfamiliar idea (AI code suggestions) to a familiar one (phone word prediction) helps students grasp the concept more easily.

questions.question: Select ALL of these that reflect responsible AI use taught across this worksheet.
options: Checking AI suggestions before using them
Letting humans make final health and creative decisions
Keeping teachers involved even when AI helps
Letting an AI make every decision with no review, as Company A suggested
questions.explanation: Checking suggestions, keeping humans in charge of health/creative decisions, and keeping teachers involved are all responsible AI practices taught in the worksheet. Company A's idea of AI deciding everything with no review is the opposite of what the worksheet recommends.

questions.question: This worksheet suggests that AI should never be used at all, in any situation.
questions.explanation: The worksheet does not reject AI use — it shows AI being helpful in many situations (fridge, Copilot, health tracking), as long as humans stay involved.

questions.question: Which best titles the main idea of this whole worksheet?
options: Humans and machines can work together, but humans should keep an active role in decisions
Machines should always be in charge of every decision
Humans should never use any smart devices
AI and humans never interact in real life
questions.explanation: This captures the worksheet's overarching theme, seen across every scenario from the fridge to Copilot to the classroom.

questions.question: Why does the worksheet ask students to explore several DIFFERENT scenarios (fridge, doorbell, story, health, teachers, coding) instead of just one?
options: To show that the same lesson about human agency and oversight applies across many different areas of life, not just one narrow situation
Because one scenario would be too easy to understand
Because each scenario teaches a completely unrelated lesson
Because the worksheet ran out of space for just one example
questions.explanation: Using multiple, varied scenarios helps students see that the lesson about human agency applies broadly across life — not just in one narrow context.

questions.question: Select ALL of these values the worksheet connects to keeping humans involved with AI.
options: Care
Trust
Responsibility
Speed above all else
questions.explanation: The worksheet connects care, trust, and responsibility to keeping humans involved (teachers' care, trusting doctors, taking responsibility for code and stories). Speed is valued too, but never presented as more important than human judgement.

questions.question: According to this worksheet, letting AI make ALL final decisions, with no human review at all, is presented as the ideal way to use technology.
questions.explanation: The worksheet consistently rejects this idea — every scenario favours humans keeping oversight, not AI making all final decisions alone.

questions.question: What is a helpful question to ask yourself the next time you use a smart app?
options: Am I still making the important decisions, or is the app doing that without me?
How much money did this app cost?
What color is the app's icon?
How many people have downloaded this app?
questions.explanation: This reflective question captures the worksheet's central habit of checking who really holds the decision-making power in any human-AI interaction.

questions.question: How does this worksheet's message connect coding, health, creativity, and teaching into one big idea?
options: In every field, AI can be a helpful assistant, but people should keep using their own judgement and stay responsible for important decisions
In every field, AI has fully replaced humans already
These fields have nothing in common at all
Only coding involves any AI at all
questions.explanation: Across coding (Copilot), health (health app), creativity (Alex's story), and teaching (Company A/B), the same idea repeats: AI assists, but human judgement and responsibility matter.

questions.question: This worksheet's overall lesson matches its title question: yes, humans do still have agency in the digital world, if they stay involved.
questions.explanation: Every scenario in the worksheet supports this conclusion — human agency remains strong in the digital world as long as people stay thoughtfully involved.
